## Background

```{r}

#| label: setup
#| message: false
#| warning: false


library(tidyverse) 
theme_set(theme_light()) 
library(brms) 
library(bayesplot) 
library(posterior) 
library(ggdist) 
library(tidybayes)
library(rmarkdown)
library(readxl)
```

This project sets out to re-analyse the data in the article “Learning Biases Underlie ‘Universals’ in Avian Vocal Sequencing” by James and Sakata (2017). The article explored whether zebra finches learned song sequences through cultural propagation or biological predispositions. They drew some connections to music and speech in humans; suggesting that the sensorimotor processes shared across a variety of vertebrates may underlie “universals” in phonological, prosodic, and musical patterns in humans.

Zebra finches bred and raised in the lab were tutored with randomised, unbiased synthesised song stimuli made to sound like zebra finch song but with no sequence consistency. The sequences consisted of five typical zebra finch song elements (“syllables”) selected from males in other lab environments. The experimentally tutored finches’ “motifs”, zebra finch songs consisting of syllables arranged into stereotyped sequences, were analysed and compared to the motifs from zebra finch populations raised in labs and tutored with species-typical song stimuli. Three variables were compared when looking at the beginning, middle and end syllables: duration, frequency and amplitude.

They found that, despite being tutored with randomised songs, the zebra finches still preferred placing syllables in particular positions in the motif; preferences that mirrored ones by zebra finches tutored with species-typical song. Table 1, taken from James & Sakata (2017), shows the mean duration, amplitude and mean frequency of the beginning, middle and end syllables in both populations of finches. Both populations show a preference for longer syllables at the beginning and end of the motif than syllables in the middle, with syllables produced at the end being longer ones produced in the beginning. This re-analysis will focus on the duration of the beginning, middle and end syllables in both populations.

## Data

*Remember to include all code and code output in the submission.*

### Read and process the data

```{r}
#| label: read data 

zebra_finch_experimentally_tutored <- read_excel("data/ZebraFinch.xlsx", sheet = 1)|>
  mutate(Group = "experimental")|>
  mutate(Position = factor(Position, levels = c("beginning", "middle", "end")))|>
  mutate(Dur = exp(logDur))
zebra_finch_species_typical <- read_excel("data/ZebraFinch.xlsx", sheet = 2)|>
  mutate(Group = "typical")|>
  mutate(BirdID = as.character(BirdID))|>
  mutate(Position = tolower(Position))|>
  mutate(Position = factor(Position, levels = c("beginning", "middle", "end")))|>
  mutate(Dur = exp(logDur))

zebra_finch <- bind_rows(zebra_finch_experimentally_tutored, zebra_finch_species_typical)|>
  mutate(Position = factor(Position, levels = c("beginning", "middle", "end")))
```

```{r}

#| label: tbl-data
#| tbl-cap: "Preview of the data"

zebra_finch |>
  select(BirdID, Position, PositionNumber, SyllableID, logDur) |>
  head(10) |>
  knitr::kable()

```

### Descriptive statistics

We find the total number of birds and the number of syllables in each group.

```{r}

#| label: number of birds per group

zebra_finch |>
  distinct(BirdID, Group) |>
  count(Group)
```

By finding the number of instances for each Position Number in each Group, we find the possible Position Numbers (Experimentally Tutored: 1-8, Species Typical: 1-10).

```{r}

#|label: number of each position number per group

zebra_finch |>
  count(Group, PositionNumber)
```

Next, we find the number of instances each syllable position occurs (beginning, middle end) in each group, calculating the proportion occurring in each group.

```{r}

#| label: instances of each syllable position

zebra_finch |>
  count(Group, Position) |>
    group_by(Group) |>
    mutate(
   tot = sum(n),
   prop = round(n / tot, 2)
  )

```

We obtain summary data (mean, sd, min, max) for the duration of syllables in each zebra finch group, data is rounded to 2dp.

```{r}

#| label: summary measures for species-typical tutored birds

DurSummaryExperimentally <- zebra_finch_species_typical |>
  group_by(Position) |>
   summarise(
   dur_mean = (mean(Dur)), dur_sd = (sd(Dur)),
   dur_min = (min(Dur)), dur_max = (max(Dur))
  )

print(DurSummaryExperimentally)

```

```{r}

#| label: summary measures for randomly tutored birds

DurSummaryRandomly <- zebra_finch_experimentally_tutored |>
  group_by(Position) |>
    summarise(
    dur_mean = (mean(Dur)), dur_sd = (sd(Dur)),
    dur_min = (min(Dur)), dur_max = (max(Dur))
  )

print(DurSummaryRandomly)

```

```{r}

zebra_finch |>
  group_by(Position) |>
  ggplot(aes(Position, logDur, fill = Group)) +
  geom_jitter(alpha = 0.08, width = 0.3) +
  facet_grid(cols = vars(Group)) +
  scale_y_continuous(limit = c(1.0, 2.75))+
  geom_violin(alpha = 0.6, width = 0.2) +
labs(x = "Syllable Position", y = "Syllable Duration (log ms)", title = "Syllable Duration in Each Syllable Position in Experimentally Tutored Group vs Species Typical Group") +
  theme(legend.position = "none")

```

## Regression modelling

```{r}

#| label: brms

Zebra_Finch_bm <- brm(
  logDur ~ Group + Position,
  family = gaussian(),
  data = zebra_finch,
  seed = 2309,
  cores = 4,
  file = "cache/zebra_finch_bm"
)

```
